source: Kang, Chen, Yoo, Lou (2023) Explainable Automated Debugging via LLM-driven Scientific Debugging (AutoSD)
finding: AutoSD forces the LLM to write hypothesis, prediction, experiment (run in a real debugger), observation, conclusion before the patch. It is the first direct build of Zeller-style scientific debugging into an LLM loop. Repair rate stays level with a plain LLM prompt.
numbers: ARHE benchmark: plausible patches 189 (AutoSD) vs 179 (plain LLM), correct 187 vs 177; template baseline 85.77 +/- 4.20 plausible. Defects4J v1.2 correct fixes 76 (AutoSD) vs 87 (plain LLM); v2.0 113 vs 110. Beats Recoder (24, 11) and finetuned InCoder (41, 28).
limits: Gain in fix rate is nil to small; the value is the explanation and the confidence signal. Plain LLM was better on Defects4J v1.2. Codex/ChatGPT-era models.
agent_relevance: The structure does not hurt repair and gives an auditable trace. Predict-then-observe is cheap to add but is not a fix-rate booster by itself.

source: Kang, Chen, Yoo, Lou (2023) Explainable Automated Debugging via LLM-driven Scientific Debugging (AutoSD)
finding: A <DONE> token emitted only when a hypothesis is confirmed by an experiment is a usable confidence signal.
numbers: Bugs with a plausible patch and <DONE>: 89% correctly fixed; plausible patch without <DONE>: 82% correct. With real execution, <DONE> solutions were 12.4 points more likely to be plausible.
limits: Difference 7 points on one benchmark; correctness hand-labelled (100 sampled patches per group on Defects4J).
agent_relevance: Use "hypothesis confirmed by observation" as a commit signal, not model self-rated confidence.

source: Kang, Chen, Yoo, Lou (2023) Explainable Automated Debugging via LLM-driven Scientific Debugging (AutoSD)
finding: Ablation: replace real debugger output with output the LLM predicts itself ("debugger hallucination"). The confirmation signal reverses.
numbers: With hallucinated execution: <DONE> solutions were 11 points LESS likely to be plausible (real execution: 12.4 points MORE likely). Share of individual runs giving a plausible patch: 73% real vs 63% hallucinated.
limits: ARHE only.
agent_relevance: Key evidence for our predict-then-observe check: the observation must come from the world, not from the model imagining it. Imagined observation inflates confidence.

source: Kang, Chen, Yoo, Lou (2023) Explainable Automated Debugging via LLM-driven Scientific Debugging (AutoSD)
finding: Failure analysis of scientific-debugging traces: many failed hypotheses fail because the experiment could not measure anything, not because the hypothesis was bad.
numbers: Of 25 cases where all hypotheses were rejected, 13 had breakpoints never hit by the test; 2/25 invalid experiment expressions; 2/25 multi-print errors that caused wrong rejection.
limits: Small N (25). Tooling specific (one print per experiment).
agent_relevance: An agent must check that its experiment can actually observe the thing (coverage check) before rejecting a hypothesis from a null result.

source: Kang, Chen, Yoo, Lou (2023) Explainable Automated Debugging via LLM-driven Scientific Debugging (AutoSD)
finding: Human study of the explanations: no speed cost, better judgement of patch correctness on most bugs, and explanations helped detect wrong patches.
numbers: 20 participants (6 professionals). Accuracy better on 5 of 6 bugs, no significant time difference; 70% wanted explanations from repair tools; 55% satisfied with the scientific-debugging format; over 90% of students said execution values raised trust.
limits: Professionals more mixed; asked for link to business logic; N=20; six patches per person.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis-observation traces help a human or second agent audit an answer.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) debug-gym: A Text-Based Environment for Interactive Debugging
finding: Giving LLM agents a real debugger (pdb: breakpoints, print) helps on SWE-bench-Lite only for strong models. Weaker models were harmed when pdb was on from the start.
numbers: SWE-bench-Lite (300 tasks, 3 runs): Claude 3.7 Sonnet rewrite-only 37.2 +/- 2.1, with pdb from start 48.4 +/- 1.6, pdb unlocked after the 5th rewrite 52.1 +/- 1.6. Llama-3.3-70B 2.4 -> 4.0 -> 4.8.
limits: Per-cell numbers for GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini and o1 not recorded (table layout garbled in text extraction); text says weaker models were hurt, o1/o3-mini/Claude helped.
agent_relevance: Tool access alone is not the scientific method. Strong models gain 11 to 15 points; weak ones do not. Unlocking observation tools after failed rewrites worked best.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) debug-gym: A Text-Based Environment for Interactive Debugging
finding: On a simple code-generation set (Aider, 133 tasks) pdb gives no clear gain; on 10 hand-made bugs needing runtime inspection (Mini-nightmare) pdb often helps.
numbers: Aider: o3-mini 95.2 (rewrite) vs 94.2 (debug). Mini-nightmare: R1-Distill models rewrite 83.3 vs debug 93.3 (Llama-70B) and 100.0 (Qwen-32B); Llama-3.2-3B 0.0 in all arms.
limits: Mini-nightmare is 10 tasks x 3 runs: standard deviations up to 14 points. Some cells hard to align from text extraction.
agent_relevance: Observation tools pay off when the bug needs runtime facts; on easy tasks they add steps.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) debug-gym: A Text-Based Environment for Interactive Debugging
finding: Authors report agents are "far from capable of using those tools in a meaningful way": minimal prompts, no hypothesis structure, 20-step history. They suspect debugging trajectories are scarce in training data.
numbers: Best agent solves about half of SWE-bench-Lite; Claude 3.7 used the most varied actions (view, listdir, pdb); o1 and Claude keep about 90% of tasks the rewrite agent solved.
limits: Agent design and prompts were deliberately minimal; no prompt optimisation.
agent_relevance: Direct invitation for a scaffold that makes the hypothesis-predict-observe cycle explicit, which debug-gym agents lacked.

source: Levin, van Kempen, Berger, Freund (2025) ChatDBG: Augmenting Debugging with LLMs
finding: ChatDBG lets GPT-4 drive a real debugger (GDB, LLDB, pdb) and answer "why?". Each added piece (richer stack, command access, targeted question, follow-up) raised success.
numbers: Python programs, 10 runs each, gpt-4-1106-preview: "why?" only 57%; targeted question 67%; plus one follow-up with no feedback 85%. About $0.12 and 25 s per query (10,000 tokens).
limits: Manual grading; small program set (scripts and notebooks); one model; baseline stack-only rate only in a figure.
agent_relevance: Letting the model inspect state beats pasting a stack trace. The gain from a content-free follow-up suggests one pass runs out of reasoning room.

source: Levin, van Kempen, Berger, Freund (2025) ChatDBG: Augmenting Debugging with LLMs
finding: Tool use detail: the model issued 0 to 12 debugger commands per run, mostly info, slice and print. A "slice" command (which code produced a value) was essential for notebooks.
numbers: C/C++ study: 36% of suggestions fixed the root cause, 55% more fixed the proximate cause.
limits: Without slice in notebooks, taking the wheel rarely helped.
agent_relevance: Tools that trace where a value came from fit the "why is x wrong" hypothesis step.

source: Zhong, Wang, Shang (2024) Debug like a Human: LLM Debugger via Verifying Runtime Execution Step by Step (LDB)
finding: LDB splits a program into basic blocks, records variable values after each block, and asks the LLM to verify each block against the task (a predict-vs-observe check per block). Real runtime values beat model-imagined traces.
numbers: HumanEval, seeds from GPT-3.5 (73.8): Self-Debugging 81.1 (+7.3), LDB 82.9 (+9.1). GPT-4 seeds (87.2): SD 88.4, LDB 89.6. Reflexion seeds (91.5): SD 92.1, LDB 95.1. Up to +9.8% across HumanEval, MBPP, TransCoder.
limits: Debugger backbone GPT-3.5; function-level programs; Self-Debugging +Trace and +Expl even failed to improve StarCoder seeds because the dry-run trace was wrong.
agent_relevance: Strong support: actual values per step, checked against intent, gives gains where model-simulated traces do not.

source: Chen, Lin, Scharli, Zhou (2024) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
finding: Self-Debugging: model runs code, then explains it line by line ("rubber duck") and uses the execution result as feedback. Explanation alone helps when no unit tests exist.
numbers: Spider text-to-SQL: +2 to 3% from explanation alone; +9% on hardest queries. TransCoder and MBPP with unit tests: up to +12%. Matches or beats baseline sampling more than 10x candidates.
limits: Most of the gain with tests comes from the execution result. Codex/GPT-3.5/GPT-4 era.
agent_relevance: Explaining without an external check gives small gains; combined with real execution it is reliable.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: Self-repair is bottlenecked by the quality of the model own diagnosis. When repair samples are counted as cost, gains are modest or absent; a stronger or human diagnosis lifts them.
numbers: GPT-4 repair with human feedback vs its own feedback: overall 52.60% vs 33.30%; Introductory 62.21 vs 42.64; Interview 45.67 vs 19.33; Competition 14.67 vs 3.67. 16 participants wrote 2 feedbacks each for 40 failing programs; 25 repairs sampled per feedback.
limits: Only 40 programs; one-hour online survey. APPS and HumanEval.
agent_relevance: The weak step is forming the right hypothesis about why it failed.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without an external signal, asking a model to review and revise its answer lowers accuracy. Earlier gains came from oracle labels telling the loop when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA: 75.8 standard -> 38.1 after one intrinsic self-correction round. GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 95.5; GPT-4 97.5.
limits: Reasoning tasks, not code with tests; prompt design contested.
agent_relevance: Re-checking without new evidence is harmful. The check must bring in a real observation or tool.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Models are bad at locating a mistake in a reasoning trace but fine at fixing it once told where. Error finding is the bottleneck.
numbers: GPT-4 mistake-finding accuracy 52.87 on the weakest-looking overall column reported in the paper; correction works well when the true mistake location is given (backtracking).
limits: Synthetic traces from PaLM 2; five tasks (BIG-Bench Mistake); not code. Exact column of 52.87 not fully verified.
agent_relevance: The localise-the-fault step is the weak link, matching the self-repair results.

source: Ni et al. (2024) NExT: Teaching LLMs to Reason about Code Execution
finding: Training on self-generated rationales that read execution traces teaches repair via execution reasoning. Zero-shot CoT over traces is poor.
numbers: PaLM 2-L fix rate: +26.1 points absolute on Mbpp-R, +14.3 on HumanEvalFix-Plus. Zero-shot CoT with traces was 7.8 points WORSE on average than plain prompt on HumanEvalFix-Plus (DeepSeek Coder 57.3 -> 30.5; StarCoder 29.3 -> 16.5); rationale correctness only about 30%.
limits: Requires training; trained model still works without traces at test time.
agent_relevance: Prompting a model to reason about traces in natural language hallucinated exceptions not in the trace. Needs hard checks.

source: Gu et al. (2024) CRUXEval: A Benchmark for Code Reasoning, Understanding and Execution
finding: Predicting what code outputs (or what input yields an output) is hard even for GPT-4: the predict step of predict-then-observe is unreliable.
numbers: GPT-4 pass@1 67% (input) and 63% (output); with CoT 75% and 81%. Best open models 47% / 44%; Code Llama 34B 50% / 46% (with CoT variants). HumanEval score does not predict CRUXEval for GPT-4-distilled models.
limits: 800 short Python functions; no multi-step bug state.
agent_relevance: Predictions are wrong 20 to 40% of the time on small functions, so a surprise from observation is common and informative.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Reasoning Runtime Behavior of a Program with LLM: How Far Are We? (REval)
finding: Four runtime-behaviour prediction tasks plus a check that answers are consistent with each other (a right output should not follow a wrong execution path).
numbers: Average accuracy across LLMs 44.4% on runtime behaviour; average Incremental Consistency score 10.3; open-source models below 20; GPT-4-Turbo highest IC.
limits: HumanEval/ClassEval adapted; no tool use.
agent_relevance: Models give right final answers with wrong intermediate reasoning, so a trace check, not only an answer check, is needed.

source: Liu et al. (2024) CodeMind: Evaluating LLMs for code reasoning
finding: Framework with input/output prediction and specification reasoning tasks, 13 LLMs, 4 benchmarks.
numbers: Performance drops for higher complexity, nested constructs, non-primitive types and intra-class dependencies.
limits: Per-model numbers not extracted; v6 dated April 2026.
agent_relevance: Prediction of execution gets worse as code looks more like real code, just where debugging is needed.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) BoxingGym: Benchmarking Automated Experimental Design and Model Discovery
finding: 10 simulated science environments test an LLM "scientist" at choosing experiments and revising theories. All tested systems struggle at both.
numbers: Models: GPT-4o, Claude-3.7-sonnet, Qwen-2.5 7B/32B, OpenThinker 7B/32B. 32B beats 7B; closed beats open; metric is Expected Information Gain regret against the best of 100 random experiments. Hyperbolic discounting stayed hard; population growth gave negative standardized error (good).
limits: Simulated models, not software; numbers mostly in figures.
agent_relevance: LLM agents under-use experiments to revise theories.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) BoxingGym: Benchmarking Automated Experimental Design and Model Discovery
finding: Prior information often made results worse after 10 experiments (models kept a strong early assumption), and fitting explicit statistical models did not reliably help. Explanations do not transfer what experiments teach.
numbers: Box Apprentice (GPT-4o plus model fitting) did not consistently beat GPT-4o and favoured overly simple forms such as linear fits; novice agents given the scientist explanation did worse than the scientist. GPT-4o had the lowest EIG regret.
limits: Same overconfidence noted by Li et al.
agent_relevance: Anchoring on an initial theory and failing to revise is the LLM form of confirmation bias; a scaffold should force a disconfirming test.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: Inductive reasoning with iterative hypothesis refinement
finding: Propose, test against data with an exact interpreter, refine. The LLM proposes well but cannot reliably apply its own rules; replacing the exact interpreter by the LLM removes most of the gain.
numbers: Task accuracy ACRE: direct prompting 28.0, self-refine with LLM as interpreter 32.0, symbolic interpreter T=1,N=1 45.0, T=3,N=5 59.0. MiniSCAN task accuracy 0.0 direct vs 46.0 (T=3,N=1). Majority vote over samples did not help (ACRE 29.0).
limits: Rule-induction benchmarks, not code; MiniARC raw accuracy got worse with refinement.
agent_relevance: Good proposer, poor tester: tests must be run by a real tool. Mirrors the AutoSD hallucinated-debugger result.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: On the Wason selection task (choosing tests that could disprove a rule) models and humans both do poorly, and both do better with realistic than arbitrary rules.
numbers: Wason accuracy lower than for natural language inference and syllogisms, for humans and models; 5-shot prompting helps Chinchilla on realistic rules but little on arbitrary ones.
limits: Older models; exact per-model numbers in figures.
agent_relevance: LMs inherit the human weakness at choosing tests that could disprove a hypothesis; abstract framing will not fix it.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang, Slivkins (2024) Can Large Language Models Explore In-Context?
finding: On bandit tasks (choose where to gather information), LLMs do not explore robustly unless the history is summarized externally.
numbers: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama2 with many prompts: only one configuration (GPT-4 + chain of thought + externally summarized history as sufficient statistics) explored satisfactorily.
limits: Simple multi-armed bandits, not debugging.
agent_relevance: Choosing which experiment to run is exploration. The agent needs a compact summarized record of tested hypotheses, not a long raw history.

source: Yao et al. (2023) ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
finding: Alternating reasoning and acting with observations is the base pattern of agent debugging loops and cuts hallucination versus reasoning alone.
numbers: Absolute success gain of 34% on ALFWorld and 10% on WebShop over imitation/RL baselines using 1 to 2 examples; in HotpotQA failure analysis chain-of-thought failures had 56% hallucination, ReAct 0%.
limits: Different domain; ReAct has more reasoning errors from repetitive loops.
agent_relevance: ReAct is the loop to which hypothesis and prediction fields would be added.

source: Bouzenia, Devanbu, Pradel (2024) RepairAgent: An Autonomous, LLM-Based Agent for Program Repair
finding: An agent with a finite state machine guiding phases (gather information, gather ingredients, validate fixes) mirrors the human interleaving of information gathering and experiments.
numbers: Fixes 164 bugs on Defects4J, including 39 not fixed by earlier techniques; 90 in Defects4J v2; average 270,000 tokens per bug.
limits: GPT-3.5 agent; lower generalisation on the GitBug-Java set.
agent_relevance: A state machine that forces phases (understand, experiment, validate) is a working scaffold.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) AutoCodeRover: Autonomous Program Improvement
finding: Fault localisation from tests (spectrum-based) sharpens code search for issue fixing.
numbers: 19% efficacy on SWE-bench-Lite (300 issues), above SWE-agent as reported at the time.
limits: Early 2024 numbers; since surpassed.
agent_relevance: Combine the hypothesis with test-derived evidence for where to look.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
finding: The interface the agent uses (small search/view/edit commands, lint guardrails, concise feedback) changes success a lot at fixed model.
numbers: GPT-4 Turbo solves 12.47% of 2,294 SWE-bench tasks vs 3.8% for the earlier best non-interactive retrieval system; on SWE-bench-Lite the ACI gives 10.7 points over a default Linux shell.
limits: Model fixed (GPT-4 Turbo); ports to Claude 3 Opus at 10.5%.
agent_relevance: Good tool feedback matters as much as the reasoning prompt.

source: Tian et al. (2024) DebugBench: Evaluating Debugging Capability of LLMs
finding: Debugging benchmark across bug types and three languages. Runtime feedback helps simple bugs but not logic bugs.
numbers: Runtime feedback consistently boosts syntax and reference errors but is unhelpful for logic errors; multiple and logic errors much harder; closed models below human level.
limits: Bugs implanted by GPT-4; zero-shot.
agent_relevance: Execution output alone does not tell the model which hypothesis to test; logic bugs need a hypothesis.
